**D Line Extension Section 1** (Wilshire/La Brea, Wilshire/Fairfax and Wilshire/La Cienega) opened on 8 May 2026, bringing heavy rail to Museum Row and the Miracle Mile for the first time. Service runs approximately from 5:00 to midnight every day, with extended late-night hours on Fridays and Saturdays.

## Los Angeles Metro Rail: the network trying to stitch together a city built for the car

Los Angeles Metro Rail is not a metro in the European sense, and it pays to understand that before stepping into your first station. Anyone arriving with Paris, Madrid, Tokyo or New York in mind will be in for a rough first day.

...

The big remaining step is the opening of the Automated People Mover, an elevated automated system that will connect LAX/MTC with the terminals without a bus.

How to reach LAX/MTC from the main tourist areas:

* **From Downtown:** A Line + C Line at Willowbrook/Rosa Parks, or E Line to Expo/Crenshaw then K Line.
* **From Santa Monica:** E Line to Expo/Crenshaw, transfer to K Line.
* **From Hollywood:** B Line to 7th Street/Metro Center, then E or A as needed.
* **From Long Beach:** A Line + C Line at Willowbrook/Rosa Parks.
* **From Pasadena:** A Line through-service to Downtown then transfer.

It is far cheaper than a taxi or Uber (a Downtown-to-LAX trip via Metro costs US$1.75 versus US$40-70 by rideshare), but not always faster. If you have lots of luggage, are travelling at night or are tight on time, give yourself margin. It is ideal for tight budgets, heavy peak-hour traffic and travellers without too many bags.

...

|Transfers |Free within 2 hours on the same TAP |

The key to the system is **fare capping** : you pay per ride until you hit the daily (US$5) or weekly (US$18) cap, after which Metro rides are included. In practice, this replaces most traditional passes. There is no longer any need to calculate how many rides you will take; what matters is that you always use the **same card or device** so the system credits the rides correctly. If you pay one day with Apple Wallet and the next with a physical TAP, the cap does not carry over.

Real-world tip: for a tourist taking three or four trips a day, the US$5 daily cap is essentially a free day from the third ride onwards. Do not buy passes in advance unless you know you will be using the network intensively for several weeks.

## Hours and frequencies

Service starts around **5:00** in the morning and ends around **23:45** or midnight depending on the line and direction.

...

" LA Metro is no worse than other major North American systems, but it is not Tokyo either: pay attention to your surroundings, particularly if you arrive used to the more sheltered European context.

## Accessibility and the first/last mile

Los Angeles Metro stations are, in general, more accessible than many older European networks: most were built under the ADA, with lifts, ramps and level platforms. Metro publishes real-time elevator status on its site and provides Access Services as complementary paratransit.

The real problem in LA is not the station itself but the **first/last mile** , the gap between the station and your final destination. Los Angeles can be hostile to pedestrians and to anyone with limited mobility: wide avenues, long crossings, relentless summer heat, lack of shade, freeways cutting through neighbourhoods. A station may be perfectly accessible while the route to your hotel feels like a small expedition. Before picking a station, also check:

...

What the network **does not yet cover well** : Beverly Hills (waiting for the next D Line sections), UCLA and Westwood (same), Griffith Observatory (needs a bus or shuttle), the Getty Center (needs a bus), Malibu (no rail), Dodger Stadium (only event-day shuttles from Union Station), Burbank Airport (not connected), Marina del Rey and many Westside employment areas. For those destinations, the sensible move is to combine Metro with bus, rideshare or car.

## Connections with other transport

The intermodal integration at Union Station is probably the best in the whole network:

* **Metrolink:** regional commuter rail to Ventura, Antelope Valley, Riverside, San Bernardino and Orange County.
* **Amtrak Pacific Surfliner:** to San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara and San Diego.
* **Amtrak Long Distance:** Coast Starlight (to Seattle), Southwest Chief (to Chicago), Sunset Limited (to New Orleans).
* **FlyAway:** direct bus from Union Station to LAX (an alternative to Metro if you have heavy luggage).
* **G Line BRT:** dedicated-lane rapid bus across the San Fernando Valley, transfer at North Hollywood.
* **J Line (Silver Line) BRT:** connects South Bay with El Monte via the I-110 and I-10.
* **Metro and municipal buses:** Big Blue Bus (Santa Monica), Culver CityBus, LADOT DASH, Foothill Transit, Long Beach Transit, Pasadena Transit and many more, all accept TAP with the EZ Transit Pass.

## Bicycles, pets and luggage

* **Bicycles:** allowed on every train at any hour (with common sense at peak). Racks are available at major stations, and Metro Bike Share operates in several neighbourhoods.
* **Scooters and skateboards:** allowed if folded or reasonably sized.
* **Pets:** only service dogs without a carrier; other animals must be in an enclosed carrier.
* **Luggage:** no specific size limit, but oversized items are tolerated with common sense. LAX/MTC has luggage carts on site.

...

Koreatown has become one of the densest, most walkable corridors in the city thanks to the D Line. The Regional Connector completely changed the dynamics of Downtown, eliminating awkward transfers and making daily trips between Santa Monica and Pasadena viable. The K Line has driven private investment in Inglewood, although with the usual contradictory effects (rising property values, gentrification, displacement). Every new station changes land values in its surroundings, attracts mixed-use residential projects and reopens the debate around densification.

For a city built on the promise of the car, every station opening is also a political statement. The D Line Extension, in particular, brings heavy rail to historically affluent neighbourhoods that for decades resisted heavy transit. Its full delivery will mark a before-and-after in how Los Angeles understands its own urban future.

## International comparison

Comparing Metro Rail with much older systems is not always fair.
Against the New York Subway (472 stations, 24 lines, 5.5 million daily riders) or Tokyo (multiple operators, thousands of stations, tens of millions of daily riders), LA looks small. But compared with mid-sized North American systems, Washington DC, Atlanta, Miami, San Francisco BART or Vancouver SkyTrain, the LA network is fully competitive and, with the current expansion, is on track to become one of the most relevant on the West Coast.

What is genuinely unusual about LA is not its length but its **rate of change** . Few systems in the world are adding so many stations and miles in a single decade as the Angeleno one. The Regional Connector, the K Line, LAX/MTC, the D Line Extension and the 2028 projects look more like the build-out of Beijing, Chengdu or Seoul than a classic North American system.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does Los Angeles actually have a metro?

Yes. It has 6 rail lines, 115 stations and around 121 miles of track.
The B and D Lines are heavy-rail subway; the A, C, E and K Lines are light rail with surface, elevated and underground sections.

### How much does the Los Angeles Metro cost?

The base fare is US$1.75. With a TAP card (or contactless payment, always using the same device), the system applies a US$5 daily cap and a US$18 weekly cap. Beyond that, rides are free. Transfers between Metro and bus are free for two hours.

### Does the metro reach LAX airport?

It reaches LAX/Metro Transit Center (K Line and C Line), which opened on 6 June 2025. From there, a free shuttle runs every 10 minutes to the terminals. The Automated People Mover, which will eventually connect the terminals directly without a shuttle, is scheduled to enter service soon.

### Which line is best for Hollywood?

The B Line.
The stations Hollywood/Western, Hollywood/Vine and Hollywood/Highland cover the whole tourist corridor, with Hollywood/Highland being the most convenient for the Walk of Fame, the TCL Chinese Theatre and the Dolby Theatre.

### How do I get to Santa Monica by metro?

Take the E Line to the Downtown Santa Monica terminus. From Downtown LA, the ride takes about 45-55 minutes, far more predictable than the I-10 in peak hour.

### Is the Los Angeles Metro safe?

It is used by hundreds of thousands of people every day and is reasonably safe, though the experience varies by hour, station and line. Metro has launched a public Safety Hub with real-time data, Transit Watch for incident reports, and programmes like Metro Ambassadors. At night and at certain stations (Westlake/MacArthur Park, parts of South Downtown), pay attention to your surroundings and pick cars with more passengers.

### Does the metro run 24 hours?

No.

...

D Line Extension Section 1, opened on 8 May 2026, reaches Wilshire/La Cienega, on the eastern edge of Beverly Hills. Sections 2 and 3, in advanced construction, will add Wilshire/Rodeo (deep Beverly Hills), Century City/Constellation, Westwood/UCLA and Westwood/VA Hospital ahead of the 2028 Olympic Games.

## Final assessment

Los Angeles Metro Rail is an imperfect, uneven and fascinating network. It does not solve all the mobility needs of a vast city, but it already connects many of the places that used to feel impossible to visit without a car: Hollywood, Santa Monica, Downtown, Long Beach, Pasadena, USC, Koreatown, Little Tokyo, Inglewood, LAX/Metro Transit Center and now Mid-Wilshire and Museum Row thanks to the D Line. Every new extension rearranges the mental geography of the city and turns destinations once isolated by traffic into reasonably reachable places.

# How to Ride Metro Rail

Metro rail is made up of six train lines, including 115 stations, each offering connections to Metro bus.

## Overview

Metro’s rail service consists of the following lines:

Icon - A line

#### A Line

Pomona to Long Beach

Icon - B Line

#### B Line

Union Station to North Hollywood

Icon - C Line

#### C Line

Norwalk to LAX/Metro Transit Center

Icon - D Line

#### D Line

Union Station to Wilshire/La Cienega

Icon - E Line

#### E Line

East Los Angeles to Santa Monica

Icon - K Line

#### K Line

Expo/Crenshaw to Redondo Beach

[View Schedules & Maps](https://www.metro.net/riding/schedules/)

## How to Pay, Board and Exit

* Arrive 10 minutes early for your train.
* Pay with a TAP, credit or debit card — physical or digital.
Learn more about [how to pay](https://www.metro.net/fares/how-to-pay/) .
* Tap on the validator or turnstile to enter the station’s platform/waiting area.
* Stand behind the yellow line and wait for the train to make a complete stop. Let others exit before entering.
* Take a seat or use handrails/handholds. Don’t lean against the train doors.
* Watch and listen for your stop. As you get closer to your destination, move towards the exiting doors. Wait for doors to open and exit, make sure you have all your belongings.
* Tap to exit at select stations
* Look both ways when crossing any train tracks.

## What is Allowed Onboard

* **Strollers** **:** Look for the decal on the outside of the car denoting the designated space for passengers with strollers.
* **Mobility Devices:** All Metro Rail lines are accessible to persons in wheelchairs. See Metro’s [Accessibility Guide](https://www.metro.net/riding/accessibility-guide/) for more information.
* **Bikes:** can be brought onto trains if space is available. Tandem, 3-wheeled or fuel powered bikes are not allowed.
* **Pets and emotional support, therapy, comfort, and companion animals:** need to secured in enclosed carriers and cannot block the aisle or a doorway, or interfere with the comfort or convenience of other riders.
* **Luggage:** Luggage and other large items have a designated space on Metro Rail. The space is usually located at the end of rail cars and is marked with a yellow decal.

## What is Not Allowed

* There is no eating or drinking allowed on platforms or trains.
* Smoking is not allowed within 20 feet of any Metro facility entrance, exit or operable window.
* Weapons, flammable materials and dangerous objects are prohibited on Metro.

[More in the Rider Guide](https://www.metro.net/safety-support/rider-guide/)

## **Metro Logo In Case of an Earthquake**

* Stay onboard the train or in the station unless Metro personnel give other instructions.
* The train operator will stop the train until the shaking stops, and keep you informed with announcements.
* Once it’s safe, the train will proceed to the next station.
* If the train cannot proceed and it’s not safe to remain where you are, the operators will assist with evacuation to a safe location.
* Learn more in Metro’s [Earthquake guide](https://www.metro.net/riding/earthquake-guide/) for riders.

The Metro even has service to LAX and many top tourist attractions. To make the most of the city, it’s a great idea to stay in a [hotel near Los Angeles Metro rail stations.](https://hotelsnearthemetro.com/hotels-near-the-metro-in-los_angeles)

Here is your complete guide to the L.A. Metro Rail System. We’ve broken the information down by subject, so you can easily scan for the information you’re looking for.

* Getting Information

## Getting Information

[Official site and trip planner](https://www.metro.net/)

[The Metro Rail Map](https://media.metro.

...

There is no central station, as all six lines run somewhat separately, although a couple may follow the same route for a section of their routes. Some suburban stations have paid or free park and ride lots and most stations have bike storage available.

Every month, an estimated 7.4 million people ride the Los Angeles Metro rail system, the 2 nd busiest in the United States (New York City subways are the busiest.)

Grand Central Station, LA

## A Rundown of Each of the Six Lines

* Red Line (subway/heavy rail): Runs from downtown’s Union Station to North Hollywood. This is the line closest to many of LA’s top attractions. It connects with the Blue, Expo and Orange (bus) lines.
* Purple Line (subway/heavy rail): Connects downtown LA to Westlake and Koreatown.
* Expo Line: Links USC and Exposition Park with Culver City, Santa Monica and downtown LA.
* Blue Line: Runs from downtown LA to Long Beach, and connects with the Green, Red and Expo lines along the way.
* Green Line: Services Norwalk and Redondo Beach, and LAX.
* Gold Line: Connects East LA to Little Tokyo, Chinatown and Pasadena via Union Station, where it connects with the Red Line.

NOTE: It should be mentioned here that the Orange Line express bus connects the San Fernando Valley to North Hollywood, and the Silver Line express bus connects El Monte regional bus station to Harbor Gateway Transit Center in Gardena. Also, DASH busses connect with many of the rail lines to take you directly to Beachwood Canyon, Downtown, Fairfax and Hollywood locations.

## What times does the metro run?

Most lines generally run from just before 5 am through midnight on weekdays, with train service until 2am on the weekends. Use the [NextTrip website](https://www.metro.net/riding/nextrip/) to find out specific arrival times.

## What is the train frequency?

During peak times, the trains run as often as every 5 minutes or so, but during off time and late at night, they run about every 15-20 minutes.

...

## How much does it cost?

A single ride to any destination is $1.75 and includes transfers for up to two hours. Day passes are $7 but are only worth it if you know you will be taking four trips more than two hours apart. Senior, disabled and student (with valid ID) day passes cost $2.50. Weekly passes are $25, and monthly passes are $100. Senior/disabled monthly passes are $20, college student monthly passes are $43, and K-12 monthly passes are $24. [Here is more information on tickets and maps.](http://www.la-electric-travel.com/los-angeles-metro-rail.html)

The TAP Card

The handy TAP card is refillable and can be used at any metro train station. They are also available for purchase at select retailers for a $2 surcharge. The cards can be filled with pre-set dollar amounts, day passes, weekly passes or monthly passes. Simply hold your TAP card against the marked terminals as you enter through the turnstiles.
Some stations don’t have turnstiles, but still make sure to tap – otherwise you could be charged a fine up to $250.

You can refill your TAP card at all metro rail stations, online or by phone. When your visit to L.A. is over, be sure to hold onto your TAP card, as it’s accepted at all 26 county transit agencies around Southern California and has a 10-year life span. You will also be able to refill your card on the [TAP website](https://www.taptogo.net/) .

Universal City, LA

## Is the metro safe?

This is one of America’s largest railway systems; it is ridden by many thousands of people every single day and is safe and clean. Just as you would with any public transport system in any major city, keep your wits about you, and be vigilant late at night. [Don’t wave around expensive items (i.e. your smartphone or wallet) if you’re sitting or standing by the doors](https://www.timeout.com/los-angeles/things-to-do/los-angeles-metro-guide) .
Common sense goes a long way with any public mode of transportation.

## Accessibility

There is disability, stroller and bike access on all Metro lines. Some stations even have bike storage for a small fee. All rail lines have direct connections to bus lines that run throughout the city.

## Can I charge my phone or connect to WiFi on the Metro?

There are no charging sockets at any of the rail stations, and no Wi-Fi currently. Smartphone users can use their cellular plans to connect online. However, the bus system in Los Angeles does have free Wi-Fi. To use the on-board bus wi-fi, connect to the network “Free Metro WiFi.” It will have a speed equivalent to 4G LTE, which is good for basic web surfing. The service is free and there is no limit on time usage.

## How crowded does it get?

The E (Expo) line is consistently the busiest. However, every line will be crowded during peak times on weekdays, which is generally 7 am – 9 am, and again from 3 pm to 6 pm.
